# DeepSeek Harness

English | [中文](README.zh.md)

DeepSeek Harness (`dsh`) is an open-source agent harness developed by [DeepSeek AI](https://deepseek.com).

It is built on an **everything-is-a-plugin** architecture and powered by [Cordis](https://github.com/cordiverse/cordis), whose design is described in [_A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.25512).

Documentation: [https://deepseek-harness.github.io/deepseek-harness/](https://deepseek-harness.github.io/deepseek-harness/)

## Developer preview

DeepSeek Harness is in _developer preview_ and iterating rapidly. **THERE WILL BE COMPATIBILITY-BREAKING CHANGES.**

Review the [safety notice](SAFETY.md) before running the project.

## Run

### Run from `npm`

Install `Node.js`, then run:

```sh
npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web
```

The command starts the Web UI at `http://127.0.0.1:3080` by default and opens it in the default browser for a local launch. An SSH launch only prints the host URL because the SSH client or editor owns the local forwarded address. Pass `--no-open` to run the server without opening a browser. See [Web UI guide](docs/user/guide/index.md).

### Run from source

To run from a repository checkout:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness.git
cd deepseek-harness
pnpm install
pnpm run build
pnpm dsh web
```

`pnpm run build` prepares the repository artifacts. `pnpm dsh web` uses those built artifacts without rebuilding.

## Community and support

- Submit feedback or bug reports through [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/discussions).
- Add the [`dsh-plugin`](https://github.com/topics/dsh-plugin) topic to your plugin repository for discoverability.
- Join DeepSeek Harness Discord community.

## Contributing

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Development

Start with the [development guide](docs/development.md) and [architecture documentation](docs/architecture.md).

`pnpm run dev:web` builds, serves, and rebuilds client bundles on source edits in one terminal, and `make help` lists the matching Make targets for Web and Desktop; the guide's application commands section owns the full table.

For agents, follow [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md).

## Zagitta/gpu-unlock (https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock)

README (start):
### Your GeForce runs AI at half speed. This fixes it.

**Up to 2× FP16 / BF16 / TF32 tensor throughput** · **+25–55% LLM prefill** · **+25–50% fine-tuning** · **+30–55% image generation**

[Supported GPUs](#supported-gpus) · [Benchmarks](#what-you-get) · [Install](#how-to-install) · [FAQ](#faq) · [Support](#support-me)

---

NVIDIA ships GeForce cards with their tensor cores capped to **half speed** for
FP16, BF16 and TF32 math with FP32 accumulation, which is what nearly all AI
training and unquantized inference uses. The same silicon sold as an RTX A-series
or professional card runs at full rate. `gpu_unlock` removes that cap at boot,
before the stock NVIDIA driver loads. No patched driver, no VBIOS flash, nothing
to redo when NVIDIA releases a new driver.

---

## Supported GPUs

| Generation                | Cards                                                                                                                  | Status                    |
| ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| **Ampere** (RTX 30)       | RTX 3050, 3060, 3060 Ti, 3070, 3070 Ti, 3080, 3080 Ti, 3090, 3090 Ti, plus RTX 3070/3080 Laptop GPUs                   | Stable, 100+ user reports |
| **Ada Lovelace** (RTX 40) | RTX 4060, 4060 Ti, 4070, 4070 SUPER, 4070 Ti, 4070 Ti SUPER, 4080, 4080 SUPER, 4090, 4090 D, RTX 4050/4060 Laptop GPUs | Experimental              |
| **Turing** (RTX 20)       | RTX 2060, 2060 SUPER, 2070, 2070 SUPER, 2080, 2080 SUPER, 2080 Ti, Titan RTX                                           | Experimental              |
| Blackwell (RTX 50)        |                                                                                                                        | Not supported             |

Laptops only stay unlocked if the dedicated GPU is never fully powered off.  
Many laptops power it down when idle, which silently resets the unlock. Turning  
off runtime power management with `options nvidia NVreg_DynamicPowerManagement=0x00`
in `/etc/modprobe.d/` helps on some models, but expect mixed results.

The exact PCI device IDs are in [`kernel/gpu_unlock/recipes.c`](kernel/gpu_unlock/recipes.c).
Linux only. For Windows see the [FAQ](#faq).

---

## What you get

The tensor core rate doubles. How much of that you see depends on how much of
your workload is FP16/BF16/TF32 matrix math, and on whether the card has the
power headroom to run it.

Dense matrix multiply (FP32 accumulation, stock power limits):

| Card | BF16 before | BF16 after | Gain |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RTX 3060 12 GB | 27 TFLOPS | 51 TFLOPS | +87% |
| RTX 3060 Ti | 37 TFLOPS | 68 TFLOPS | +82% |
| RTX 3070 | 40 TFLOPS | 72 TFLOPS | +81% |
| RTX 3080 10 GB | 65 TFLOPS | 113 TFLOPS | +73% |
| RTX 3090 | 75 TFLOPS | 125 TFLOPS | +65% |
| RTX 3090 Ti (450 W) | 88 TFLOPS | 157 TFLOPS | +80% |
| RTX 4070 Ti | 81 TFLOPS | 150 TFLOPS | +84% |
| RTX 4080 | 104 TFLOPS | 193 TFLOPS | +87% |
| RTX 4090 | 165 TFLOPS | 329 TFLOPS | +100% (peak MMA rate) |

The RTX 4090 runs out of power before it runs out of tensor cores, so large
GEMMs at stock power limits gain much less than the peak rate suggests.

Real workloads:

| Workload | Typical speedup |
| --- | --- |
| LLM prefill / prompt processing, FP16/BF16 or AWQ/GPTQ (vLLM, PyTorch, Transformers) | +25–55% |
| Time to first token | 25–30% lower |
| LoRA and full fine-tuning in BF16 | +25–50% |
| Image generation, FP16/BF16 (SDXL, SD 1.5, Krea, DiT models in ComfyUI) | +30–55% |
| Video generation, BF16 compute (Wan 2.2) | +15–20% |
| FlashAttention / SDPA kernels | +50–60% |
| llama.cpp / Ollama with quantized GGUF | 0–15%, mostly at long context |
| LLM decode / token generation (memory bound) | No change |
| INT8, FP8 and INT4 models | No change |
| Gaming and FP32 CUDA | No change |

Outputs are bit-identical before and after; only the speed changes. These
numbers come from the [compatibility reports](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock/issues)
users have filed, where you can find full benchmark details and post your own.

---

## How to install

First run:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock
cd gpu-unlock
make install
```

Then append `gpu_unlock.targets=all` to your kernel command line, keeping
existing options:

- **GRUB (Debian/Ubuntu/Mint):** add it inside `GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT`
in `/etc/default/grub`, then run `sudo update-grub`.
- **GRUB (Arch/CachyOS):** same edit, then run
`sudo grub-mkconfig -o /boot/grub/grub.cfg`.
- **Fedora/RHEL:** run
`sudo grubby --update-kernel=ALL --args="gpu_unlock.targets=all"`.
- **systemd-boot:** append it to the `options` line in your boot entry
(`bootctl status` shows its location).
- **UKI / generated entries:** add it to `/etc/kernel/cmdline` and regenerate
your boot images/entries (e.g. `sudo mkinitcpio -P` for mkinitcpio UKIs).

# FAQ

- Q: Do you have a website/coin/installer?  
A: No this is the one and only OG source for gpu-unlock. Crypto, websites, installers and what else is not associated with this project or the developer in any way shape or form. 
- Q: Does this depend on a specific driver version? I see `610.43.03` is pinned.  
A: No the driver is only fetched to extract firmware this unlock depends on    
- Q: What about Windows?  
A: I don't run windows and don't plan to maintain it but [https://github.com/impacifist/Windows-GPU-UNLOCK](https://github.com/impacifist/Windows-GPU-UNLOCK) has built a port, YMMV.   
There are windows installer's floating around but I would recommend being ++**very**++ careful with those.
- Q: What about Blackwell (RTX 50)?  
A: Not supported and unlikely to happen.    
- Q: Why did Nvidia handicap my GPU?  
A: Market segmentation, they want businesses to purchase the professional cards without these limitations at significantly higher prices.
- Q: Does this hurt my GPU?  
A: It's very unlikely, this only unlocks a small handicap Nvidia has put in place to differentiate datacenter and professional cards from consumer versions. It may heat up your GPU slightly because it now does more compute but the standard throttling and power management remains completely intact and should downclock.    
- Q: How can I assist?  
A: Please consider [donating](#support-me) so I can purchase more GPUs <3

## Local build

Every build downloads the NVIDIA/CachyOS inputs over HTTPS and generates
firmware only in the build directory and the binary package. All three formats install through the same `make install-*`
targets. Packages are built from the working tree, uncommitted changes included.

Build, install build dependencies, and install the packages in one step
(asks for your sudo password):

```sh
make install        # detect the distribution and select an installer
make install-arch   # makepkg -sif
make install-deb    # apt-get build-dep, dpkg-buildpackage, apt-get install
make install-rpm    # dnf builddep, rpmbuild, dnf install
```

`make install` uses `/etc/os-release` (`ID`, then `ID_LIKE`) to detect Arch,
Debian/Ubuntu, or Fedora/RHEL/CentOS families. The RPM installer requires DNF.
For other distributions, select a compatible explicit target above.

`make arch`, `make deb` and `make rpm` only build. Debian and RPM packages go
to `build/deb` and `build/rpm`. The NVIDIA inputs are cached in
`~/.cache/gpu-unlock/inputs` (`make inputs`; override with `INPUTS=`).
`dpkg-buildpackage` itself never uses the network, so a clean-chroot build (sbuild or
pbuilder) needs `GPU_UNLOCK_INPUTS` pointing at that cache.
The `make dist` archive, the Debian source package and the `.nosrc.rpm`
contain no NVIDIA archives or generated firmware.

## How it works

This Linux kernel module combines the cmpunlocker's V67/PLM technique with the
pre-driver timing of the UEFI approach. At boot it runs the unlock, writes the
speed selectors (SS0 `0x88888888`, which selects the full BF16 rate, and the
4-bit SS1 `0x8` IMLA4) and performs an FLR before the unmodified NVIDIA driver
binds the card. It is neither a UEFI application nor a patched NVIDIA driver.

## Boot flow and opt-in

The packages put `gpu_unlock` and its firmware in the initramfs and load it
there, before `nvidia` can bind a card:

- **mkinitcpio:** `/etc/mkinitcpio.conf.d/zz-gpu-unlock.conf` inserts
`gpu_unlock` right before `nvidia` in `MODULES`, so a display card is blank
for as short a time as possible. Without `nvidia` in the image, it goes
last and still runs before an `nvidia` loaded from the root filesystem.
Images are rebuilt on install. mkinitcpio ignores drop-ins for an image
built with `-c ` or a preset `_config`; put `gpu_unlock` right
before `nvidia` in that config's `MODULES` yourself.
- **initramfs-tools:** `/usr/share/initramfs-tools/modules.d/gpu-unlock.conf`.
- **dracut:** `/usr/lib/dracut/dracut.conf.d/gpu-unlock.conf`.

With initramfs-tools and dracut, the module is built for every installed
kernel that has headers, and those kernels' images are rebuilt on install
and again on removal. Kernels installed later get the module and a new
image from the kernel's own install hooks.

There is no `softdep nvidia pre:` rule: kmod honours only the first
`softdep nvidia` line it reads, so other packages' rules (`nvidia-utils`,
`gddr6_hwmon`) would silently override it, or it would override theirs.

The module does nothing unless the kernel command line opts in:

```
gpu_unlock.targets=all                          # every supported unbound card
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0                 # only these cards
gpu_unlock.targets=0000:21:00.0,0000:22:00.0    # comma-separated
```

Addresses are full PCI names as `lspci -D` prints them (hex digits in either
case), independent of GPU numbering and display role. An entry that is not
a supported card (see [Supported GPUs](#supported-gpus)), including `all` mixed with addresses, is logged and ignored.
The cards are unlocked concurrently, about a second in all however many
there are, and each on its own: a card that is already bound or powered
down is skipped. Bus mastering that the board firmware left on (Supermicro
X11 does this whatever its option ROM and bus master settings) is cleared
first; a card some driver already initialised is still refused. Then
`nvidia` loads and binds every card as usual.

The display card works too. Its firmware framebuffer (the boot console and
Plymouth) keeps running while the unlock's firmware steps run, and is
removed just before the card's reset, as `nvidia-drm` would do a moment
later anyway. Its screen is blank from that reset until `nvidia-drm` takes
over.

Loading the module by hand after boot does nothing to a card that `nvidia`
has bound.

Suspend to RAM powers the cards off, which resets the speed selectors. After
resume the module unlocks every card it unlocked at boot again, before
`nvidia` resumes it: its suspend notifier runs just ahead of the one `nvidia`
resumes its cards from (`NVreg_UseKernelSuspendNotifiers=1`, the default in
current drivers; `nvidia-resume.service` runs later still). This adds about a
second to resume. A card that kept power, as in suspend to idle, is still
unlocked and is only read. A card that `nvidia` has already resumed, or that is
bound to another driver, is left as it is, and the log says why. Add
`gpu_unlock.resume=0` to the kernel command line, or write `0` to
`/sys/module/gpu_unlock/parameters/resume`, to turn this off. Hibernation is
not covered.

Check the result with:

```sh
journalctl -k -b | grep gpu_unlock
lspci -nnk -s 0000:[ID]:00.0
```

To stop unlocking, remove `gpu_unlock.targets=` from the kernel command line;
for a one-off boot, delete it in the bootloader's edit screen. Removing the
packages also removes the module and the initramfs drop-ins.

If the firmware on a card never stops, the module logs it and keeps the DMA
buffers that firmware may still use until the next power off. Power off
before trying again.

## 这是什么

[AIHOT](https://aihot.news) 是我做的一个 AI 热点网站。它每天从一批信源里收资料，用大模型先筛一遍、再独立打两次分，挑出真正值得看的，写成中文标题和摘要；把不同来源说的同一件事聚成一个事件，按有多少人在说排出热点；每天早上出一份日报。

这个仓库是它的引擎和框架：网站、后台、精选流程、聚簇和热度算法，**所有提示词的原文和入选门槛**，都在这里。

## 为什么开源

这半年，很多做法律、做 HR、做金融、做贵金属的朋友问我，能不能也给他们的行业做一个。

我做不了。我不懂你们的行业，不知道哪些信源有用，也不知道什么样的消息，对你们来说才叫热点。

但你们懂。

- **我不是专业的开发者。** 我是设计师出身，半年前还看不太懂代码。这套代码是我和 AI 一起重写的，比以前干净了很多，但一定还有写得不好的地方。发现问题欢迎提 Issue，我不一定能很快回复，先说声抱歉。

## 它是怎么工作的

  
  

一条资料从信源进来，先判重，再预筛；可能重要的独立打两次分，写好中文标题和摘要，和别的报道聚成事件，算进热度。X 帖子没有正文或只有链接时，保留原帖的链接和图片，不调用写作或翻译模型。分数过了门槛、又不是精选里已有新闻的重复，才进精选；日报按规则编出当天要闻，周报、月报再从日报里汇编。每一步的提示词都在 [`industry/prompts/`](industry/prompts/)，改标准不用改代码。详见 [精选与校准](docs/selection.md)。

### 聚簇与热点

  
  

同一件事，官网发一篇、媒体转十篇、X 上吵一天，读者只需要看到一次。AIHOT 把它们聚成一个**事件**：先用标题摘要的向量（没配向量服务时比文字重合度）在最近两周里找候选，再让模型判断是同一件事、后续进展，还是两件事；拿不准的合并，写入前再让模型复核一遍（复核可以单独换一家模型，设 `GROUP_REVIEW_MODEL`）。

**热度**按事件算，不按文章算：48 小时内，每个独立来源只算一次，24 小时减半。重复抓取不会多算，一家媒体发十篇也只算一次，所以排在前面的，是真正有很多人在说的事。

# RTX 3070 Ti Laptop GPU – gpu-unlock benchmark

A reproducible before/after benchmark of [Zagitta/gpu-unlock](https://github.com/Zagitta/gpu-unlock) on an
NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070 Ti **Laptop** GPU (GA104, `10de:24e0`) in an HP Omen 16-k0620ng. gpu-unlock is a Linux kernel module that removes the
half-rate limit on FP16/BF16/TF32 tensor-core math with FP32 accumulation on GeForce Ampere cards. Other laptop GPUs have been
reported in the gpu-unlock issues (#88, #103); this is the first GA104 laptop result.

The suite runs an identical test list twice, once on the stock card (**baseline**) and once with gpu_unlock active
(**unlocked**). It then produces a report with validity checks, all raw logs and SHA-256 checksums.

## Results at a glance

  
  

| Workload | Stock | Unlocked | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| BF16 matrix multiply 8192³ (FP32 acc.) | 33.5 TFLOPS | 50.2 TFLOPS | **+50 %** |
| FP16 matrix multiply 8192³ (FP32 acc.) | 34.0 TFLOPS | 52.3 TFLOPS | **+54 %** |
| TF32 matrix multiply 8192³ | 16.9 TFLOPS | 25.5 TFLOPS | **+51 %** |
| LLM prompt processing, 2048 tokens (BF16) | 15,452 tok/s | 22,200 tok/s | **+44 %** |
| GPT-124M training (BF16) | 20,318 tok/s | 26,232 tok/s | **+29 %** |
| LLM token generation, batch 1 | 148 tok/s | 150 tok/s | +1 % |

### Same power, more work: efficiency

The laptop GPU sits at its power cap (≈ 105 W enforced) under tensor load in both phases. gpu-unlock does not
raise that cap. The card draws the same ~103 W and runs at a **lower** SM clock (1,459 → 1,099 MHz in the sustained
test), yet finishes **48 % more work**, because each tensor-core instruction now completes at the full rate.

- **+48 % work per watt** in the 3-minute sustained BF16 load, **−33 % energy** per unit of work
- **−30 % energy per token** for LLM prompt processing: 1.85 Wh → 1.29 Wh per million prompt tokens
- Less heat for the same job, and more work per battery charge

  
  

**Trustworthy comparison.** Every validity check passed: same driver, kernel, software and power cap. Control
tests (FP32, INT8, memory bandwidth) stayed unchanged within ±2.1 %. GEMM outputs are bit-identical in both phases,
and repeat runs of both phases (the stock repeat in a separate boot) reproduced the headline results within 1 % (every test within 1.7 %).

**Full report** with every test, power/thermal data and raw logs: [series 1 – PyTorch](reports/series1-pytorch/report.md)  
### Series 2: llama.cpp with real GGUF models

One model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct) in four weight formats, all created from the same BF16 file, measured with
`llama-bench` (7 repetitions, all layers on the GPU, flash attention off and on).

  
  

| Prompt processing, 2048 tokens, flash attention on | Stock | Unlocked | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| BF16 | 3,902 tok/s | 4,983 tok/s | **+28 %** |
| F16 | 5,049 tok/s | 5,056 tok/s | +0.1 % |
| Q8_0 | 5,449 tok/s | 5,515 tok/s | +1.2 % |
| Q4_K_M | 5,119 tok/s | 5,235 tok/s | +2.3 % |
| Token generation, all formats | | | within ±1.1 % |

**Only BF16 models benefit.** llama.cpp computes BF16 weights with FP32 accumulation, which is exactly the path
gpu-unlock opens. Stock BF16 is 23 % slower than F16 at prompt processing; unlocked, it is on par. F16 weights use FP16
accumulation, which was never rate-limited on GeForce. Q8_0 and Q4_K_M run on INT8 kernels. Across these formats prompt
processing moves by −5.4 to +2.8 % (one F16 outlier with flash attention off, the rest within ±3 %). **For everyday quantized GGUF use (Ollama, LM Studio) the unlock brings no measurable gain**; the
benefit is in BF16 and PyTorch workloads (series 1). All 16 validity checks passed (same llama.cpp build,
SHA-256-identical model files).

**Full report:** [series 2 – llama.cpp](reports/llamacpp/series2-llamacpp/report.md)

## What is measured

| Category | Tests | Expected effect |
|---|---|---|
| Correctness | FP16/BF16/TF32/FP32 2048³ GEMM output hash + error vs FP64 (also verifies the TF32 switch) | identical |
| GEMM | FP16, BF16, TF32 at 2048/4096/8192 | **gain** |
| GEMM controls | FP32 (CUDA cores, TF32 off), INT8 (`torch._int_mm`) | none |
| Memory | 1 GiB device copy | none (control) |
| Kernels | SDPA attention fwd / fwd+bwd, 3×3 convolution (cuDNN) | gain / partial |
| LLM | prompt processing 512/2048 tokens, token generation batch 1 and 16 (synthetic ~0.95 B Llama-style model) | gain / info / partial |
| Training | GPT-style 124 M (BF16 and FP16), ResNet-50 (BF16) | gain / partial |
| Inference | ResNet-50 FP16; optional Stable Diffusion via diffusers | partial / gain |
| Sustained | BF16 8192³ GEMM for 180 s in 5 s windows | gain; shows power/thermal limits |

Every throughput test is warmed up, then measured as 5 samples of about 2 s each with CUDA events. Before each test
the GPU idles until it is at or below 55 °C. Power, clocks, temperature and NVML throttle reasons are logged at 10 Hz.
Control tests, which must not change, confirm that the two boots differ only in the unlock.

# MuckScraper

### A self-hosted news aggregator with multi-source grouping and local LLM analysis

> **TL;DR:** MuckScraper pulls news from multiple sources, groups related articles into stories, scores outlet bias, and generates local AI summaries and deeper reports on your own hardware.

---

## Try It First

- **[sample.muckscraper.news](https://sample.muckscraper.news)**: a public, read-only copy of this app, refreshed after every fetch run. It is what you get when you install it, minus the scraped article text (summaries and links to the publishers only).
- **[MuckScraper.news](https://muckscraper.news)**: a newspaper-style site built on the same pipeline. It publishes two balanced editions of 20 stories a day. The newspaper layer is not part of this repo; the aggregator it is built on is.

---

## What It Does

MuckScraper gathers and breaks down the news so you don't have to read the same story twelve times, unless you want to. A few times a day it pulls in articles from RSS feeds (and NewsAPI/GNews if you have keys), works out which ones are about the same event, and turns each pile into a single story. Each story gets one headline, a summary, a look at how the left, center and right are covering it, and a link to every source.

---

## Why It's Different

Most aggregators hand you a list of links. MuckScraper is built around stories, and it does the work on your own machine.

- **One story, every outlet.** Each new article is turned into an embedding (`nomic-embed-text`, stored in pgvector) and compared with recent stories. Close calls get a quick yes/no from the model. Twelve outlets reporting "Senate passes the bill" end up as one story instead of twelve links. Wire copies, where the same AP text runs under three mastheads, are spotted by text overlap and counted once.
- **Bias you can see.** Every outlet carries a left-to-right rating, from AllSides where they rate it and from the model where they don't. Each story shows how many left, center and right outlets covered it, and if one side trails, there's a button to go fetch more from it.
- **Summaries of real reporting.** The model summarizes and compares articles that reporters wrote; it never writes the news. A deep report sets out how the left, center and right are each covering the story, what's contested and what's missing. Guardrails throw out cut-off summaries and model errors posing as headlines, and a quality report flags any figure that doesn't appear in the sources.
- **Opinion in its own lane.** Op-eds never count as news coverage. They're kept separately, linked to the story they argue about, and summed up side by side.
- **Editions, not an endless feed.** Twice a day it picks a balanced edition of 20 stories, holding back repeats unless there's real new coverage. Every past edition stays readable.
- **It's yours, and so is your reading.** It runs in Docker on your own hardware, with Ollama by default. No subscriptions, no ads. Check existing captures

An offline compatibility checker explains whether existing probe captures fit the automatic local-profile route and what is missing. It needs only Python 3.10+ and runs no probe or unlock:

python -I research/profile/check-compatibility.py "D:\RTX3090-UNLOCK"

A candidate still needs profile generation, host tests and hardware validation. An out-of-scope result does not rule out an exact existing fixed profile. Use --json for a reviewed-shareable report with limited model/topology observations; paste it into the optional offline report field in a compatibility issue. The guide also covers comparing two reports to investigate common differences.

Implementation and boundaries

The GPU family layer shares reviewed GA102/GA104/GA106 traits and identical firmware templates, while exact card/platform pins remain separate. Existing profile names and support scope are unchanged.

Headless is a separate compile-time profile. Exact GPU/PROM/PCI state, firmware driver code, ownership, cold state, immutable selectors and cleanup checks remain. The child logs to files only and rejects physical GOP reappearance or changed console/input interfaces. Ordinary builds retain their AMD display guards. Do not remove checks or substitute a PROM hash to force another machine through.

Path	Purpose
internal-boot/, research/headless/	Internal/headless source, local build, installation and host tests
unlock/, release/	Preserved legacy USB manual implementation and historical artifacts
benchmark/, evidence/	Measurement tools and selected public evidence

No VBIOS flashing or Windows driver replacement is part of the procedure. Driver 617.14 was unchanged in the documented run. Host mock tests do not add hardware support. New systems require compatibility reporting and portability validation. A machine inside the hardware-proven envelope can build and test its own local profile with the new-machine pipeline. This experimental workflow inventories NVIDIA display devices, but deep capture is limited to one reviewed RTX 3090 / 3090 Ti, RTX 3060 12GB, RTX 3060 Ti 24c9 or RTX 3070 2484 identity in the reviewed PCI/BAR state. The generic probe also records optional parent PCI information when its observation conditions match, helping investigate motherboard differences. This does not enable an unlock or correct PCI state. A generated local profile does not add another verified machine profile. USB write builds require all 22 host jobs, including fresh PCI identity checks, input policy and the topology-specific complete driver-release replay, and unchanged profile, fixtures and build inputs; hardware validation is still required. Within this envelope the generic probe discovers the bus automatically and the generated profile pins it per machine. An optional -TargetBus constrains discovery and resumed captures. LOCAL discovery also accepts captured PNP0A03/PNP0A08 root identities and up to 16 PCI path nodes, pinning the complete ancestry and checking the exact PCI parent. This experimental bridge-chain support still requires per-machine validation. LOCAL discovery and generation can pin a unique target on any 16-bit PCI segment. Prepare, release and PCI access must match that segment as well as the captured bus; nonzero-segment operation is experimental and still needs physical validation. Single-RTX systems may have no iGPU or separate EDID driver on the non-aggregate path. Without a separate EDID driver, non-aggregate LOCAL generation/replay accepts one to four unique NVIDIA display children. Three/four-child paths remain experimental; four-child coverage is host-only. EDID-driver and aggregate generation retain a two-child limit. Recognized AMI aggregate consoles with one or two display children can generate an experimental local profile and require their own prepare/release replay; this does not establish another hardware success. Multiple NVIDIA GPUs are not generated. Staging the unlock package needs -StageUnlock.
